plan.opening_note: My notes say decode already has an inlined fast path for bytes alphabets that folds four digits per step, and that small chunk tweaks hardly move the metric. So this time I'll look for a structural change in b58decode, such as folding more digits per step or a cheaper bigint-to-bytes conversion, rather than more micro-tuning.

actions.reason: The decode loop no longer accounts for enough of decode_ir to reach the 1% minimum. Folding eight digits per step measured ratio 0.9989, a saving of about 240 instructions per call. Mapping native 16-bit digit pairs through a table measured 1.0218, which is worse because of the per-element C-call overhead. Most of the decode benchmark's instructions go to payload generation and the benchmark's own pure-Python reference encoder, so the library's share is only a few percent of the total. Getting 1% would mean roughly halving the library's per-call cost, and I did not find a change that does that.

worker_outcome: no candidate: the session stopped without submitting a change [stop: gave up; model calls: 6]

journal.text:
I tried two rewrites of the decode loop in base58/__init__.py to cut decode_ir. The first mapped native 16-bit digit pairs through a lookup table. The second folded eight digits per step into the accumulator. Both edits sat around lines 183-205, plus a helper line near line 12 that I later removed.

The pair table measured decode_ir ratio 1.0218 (parent 2521839902, candidate 2576776066), so it was worse, apparently from per-element C-call overhead. Folding eight digits measured 0.9989 (candidate 2519013398), against a required 0.9900. Both runs were rejected as no_improvement. Equivalence was identical and guards were ok in both. I submitted no candidate.

I now believe the decode loop is no longer a large enough share of decode_ir to reach a 1% cut. Most of the benchmark's instructions go to payload generation and harness work, not to the loop.

Next I should profile where decode_ir actually spends its instructions before I touch the loop again. I should also look at whether input validation or the leading-zero handling costs more than the arithmetic does.
